Medicine 09.question: ১) NS1 viral antigen is related to which infection?
Medicine 09.exp:
NS1 (Non-structural protein 1) antigen is a specific viral marker associated with dengue virus infection. It can be detected in the blood during the early phase of dengue illness, usually from the first day of fever and often within the first week. Detection of NS1 antigen helps in early diagnosis of dengue infection, before antibodies such as IgM and IgG become detectable. NS1 is a secreted glycoprotein involved in dengue viral replication and immune response. It is not associated with rabies, HIV/AIDS, or hepatitis viruses.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • NS1 antigen → Dengue virus infection.

  • Detectable during the early febrile phase of dengue.

  • IgM antibody appears after several days and indicates recent infection.

  • IgG antibody suggests past exposure or secondary infection.

  • Dengue virus belongs to the Flavivirus family.

Exam Pearl:
Early dengue diagnosis = NS1 antigen detection; later diagnosis = IgM/IgG antibody detection.

Medicine 09.question: ২) What is confirmatory test for TB?
Medicine 09.exp:
Gene Xpert (Xpert MTB/RIF assay) is considered a confirmatory diagnostic test for tuberculosis (TB) because it directly detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA in clinical specimens and also identifies rifampicin resistance. It is a rapid molecular test that provides results within a short time compared with conventional culture methods. Sputum cytology is not used for TB diagnosis, chest X-ray (CXR) only supports the diagnosis but is not confirmatory, and the Mantoux test (MT/PPD) indicates exposure or immune sensitization but cannot confirm active TB disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gene Xpert → Detects MTB DNA + rifampicin resistance.

  • Gold standard for TB diagnosis: Mycobacterial culture (though slow).

  • Mantoux test: Indicates TB exposure, not active disease confirmation.

  • CXR: Supportive investigation, not diagnostic confirmation.

  • Sputum smear detects acid-fast bacilli (AFB) but has lower sensitivity.

Exam Pearl:
For rapid confirmation of active TB in MCQs: Gene Xpert (Xpert MTB/RIF) is the best answer.

Medicine 09.question: ৩) Which is known as Hansen's disease?
Medicine 09.exp:
Hansen's disease is the medical name for leprosy, a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, mucosa of the upper respiratory tract, and eyes. The disease is characterized by loss of sensation due to peripheral nerve involvement, skin lesions, and possible deformities if untreated. The immune response determines the clinical spectrum, ranging from tuberculoid leprosy (strong cell-mediated immunity, few bacilli) to lepromatous leprosy (weak immunity, numerous bacilli). Malaria, dengue, and tuberculosis are caused by different organisms and are not called Hansen's disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hansen's disease = Leprosy.

  • Causative organism: Mycobacterium leprae.

  • Mainly affects:

    • Skin

    • Peripheral nerves

    • Eyes

  • Tuberculoid leprosy: Few bacilli, strong immunity.

  • Lepromatous leprosy: Many bacilli, weak immunity.

Exam Pearl:
Hansen's disease = Leprosy = Mycobacterium leprae infection.

Medicine 09.question: ৪) How enteric fever is transmitted?
Medicine 09.exp:
Enteric fever (typhoid fever) is transmitted mainly by the fecal-oral route through ingestion of food or water contaminated with Salmonella Typhi (and occasionally S. Paratyphi). Infected individuals shed bacteria in their feces, and transmission commonly occurs due to poor sanitation, contaminated food handlers, or unsafe drinking water. The organism invades the intestinal mucosa and spreads through the bloodstream, causing systemic illness. It is not transmitted by sexual contact, blood contamination, or respiratory droplets.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Enteric fever organism: Salmonella Typhi.

  • Transmission: Fecal-oral route.

  • Source: Contaminated food and water.

  • Humans are the only natural reservoir.

  • Chronic carriers may harbor bacteria in the gallbladder.

Exam Pearl:
Typhoid spreads by the fecal-oral route: contaminated food or water → Salmonella Typhi infection.

Medicine 09.question: ৫) Ghon focus is primary lesion of......?
Medicine 09.exp:
A Ghon focus is the primary lesion of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is a small area of caseating granulomatous inflammation usually located in the subpleural region of the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe of the lung. When the Ghon focus is associated with involvement of the draining hilar lymph nodes, it forms a Ghon complex, which represents primary pulmonary TB. Malaria, dengue, and leprosy do not produce a Ghon focus.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ghon focus → Primary pulmonary TB.

  • Ghon complex = Ghon focus + hilar lymph node involvement.

  • Organism: Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

  • Histology: Caseating granuloma with epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells.

  • Primary TB commonly affects children and previously unexposed individuals.

Exam Pearl:
Ghon focus is the classic primary lung lesion of tuberculosis; add hilar lymph nodes to get Ghon complex.

Medicine 09.question: ৬) Cardinal features of leprosy excludes.....?
Medicine 09.option3: acid fast bacilli on skin smear
Medicine 09.exp:
The cardinal features of leprosy (Hansen's disease) include anaesthetic skin lesions, thickened peripheral nerves with sensory loss, and demonstration of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) in skin slit smear. These findings are used for diagnosis of leprosy. Lymphadenopathy may occur, especially in lepromatous leprosy, but it is not considered a cardinal diagnostic feature. Leprosy primarily affects the skin and peripheral nerves due to infection with Mycobacterium leprae.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cardinal signs of leprosy:

    • Anaesthetic skin lesion

    • Thickened peripheral nerve with sensory loss

    • AFB in skin smear

  • Organism: Mycobacterium leprae.

  • Lepromatous leprosy → Numerous bacilli and more systemic involvement.

  • Tuberculoid leprosy → Few bacilli and strong cell-mediated immunity.

Exam Pearl:
Leprosy diagnosis is based on skin lesions, nerve involvement, and AFB demonstration—not lymphadenopathy.

Medicine 09.question: ৭) Low grade fever, evening rise of temperature with weight loss indicates.....?
Medicine 09.exp:
A low-grade fever with evening rise of temperature, chronic cough, and weight loss is a classic presentation of tuberculosis (TB). The evening rise in temperature occurs due to the chronic inflammatory response associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Pulmonary TB commonly presents with prolonged cough, fever, night sweats, anorexia, and weight loss. Malaria typically causes intermittent fever with chills and rigors, dengue presents with acute high-grade fever and systemic symptoms, and leprosy primarily affects the skin and peripheral nerves rather than causing this typical constitutional pattern.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • TB symptoms:

    • Evening rise of temperature

    • Weight loss

    • Night sweats

    • Chronic cough

  • Organism: Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

  • Primary TB lesion: Ghon focus.

  • Diagnosis: Molecular tests such as Gene Xpert and culture.

Exam Pearl:
Evening rise of fever + weight loss = Think tuberculosis.

Medicine 09.question: ৮) Stool dark field microscopy of which organism shows the typical ‘shooting star’ motility?
Medicine 09.exp:
Vibrio cholerae shows a characteristic “shooting star” motility on dark-field microscopy due to its rapid, darting movement produced by a single polar flagellum. This feature is classically described in cholera diagnosis. V. cholerae is a curved, comma-shaped, gram-negative bacillus that causes acute watery diarrhea (rice-water stool) through production of cholera toxin, which increases cAMP in intestinal epithelial cells leading to excessive chloride and water secretion. Salmonella Typhi, E. coli, and Entamoeba histolytica do not show this characteristic motility pattern.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • V. cholerae → “Shooting star” motility on dark-field microscopy.

  • Has a single polar flagellum.

  • Causes rice-water diarrhea.

  • Cholera toxin → activates adenylate cyclase → ↑ cAMP → chloride and water secretion.

  • Diagnosis can be supported by stool culture.

Exam Pearl:
Shooting star motility on dark-field microscopy = Vibrio ch

Medicine 09.question: ৯) What is the duration of treatment of multibacillary leprosy?
Medicine 09.exp:
Multibacillary (MB) leprosy is treated with multidrug therapy (MDT) for 12 months according to standard WHO recommendations. The MB regimen consists of rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone. MB leprosy includes patients with a higher bacillary load, multiple skin lesions, or positive slit-skin smear. Prolonged treatment is required to eliminate Mycobacterium leprae and prevent relapse and drug resistance. Earlier regimens used longer durations, but the currently accepted standard duration for MB leprosy is 12 months.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • MB leprosy treatment duration: 12 months.

  • Drugs in MDT:

    • Rifampicin

    • Clofazimine

    • Dapsone

  • MB leprosy → higher bacillary load.

  • Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy → shorter treatment duration.

Exam Pearl:
Multibacillary leprosy = MDT for 12 months (Rifampicin + Clofazimine + Dapsone).

Medicine 09.question: ১০) Millet seed type lesion in CXR is found in which type of TB?
Medicine 09.exp:
Miliary tuberculosis is characterized by multiple tiny, uniform nodules throughout both lung fields on chest X-ray, giving a classic “millet seed” appearance. This occurs due to hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from a primary or reactivated focus to multiple organs, including the lungs. The lesions are typically 1–3 mm in size and resemble millet seeds. Primary TB usually produces a Ghon focus, while secondary/post-primary TB commonly affects the upper lobes and may show cavitation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Miliary TB → Millet seed appearance on CXR.

  • Caused by hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

  • Lesions: Multiple tiny bilateral nodules (1–3 mm).

  • Can involve:

    • Lungs

    • Liver

    • Spleen

    • Bone marrow

    • Meninges

Exam Pearl:
“Millet seed” nodules on chest X-ray = Miliary tuberculosis.

Medicine 09.question: ১১) Which disease has 100% mortality?
Medicine 09.exp:
Rabies is considered a disease with almost 100% mortality once clinical symptoms appear. It is caused by the rabies virus (a Lyssavirus) and affects the central nervous system, producing progressive encephalitis. After the onset of symptoms, there is no effective curative treatment, and death usually occurs due to respiratory or neurological complications. However, rabies is preventable through timely post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), including wound care, rabies vaccine, and immunoglobulin when indicated. Dengue, AIDS, and hepatitis can be severe and fatal but do not have 100% mortality.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Rabies → Nearly 100% fatal after symptom onset.

  • Virus: Rabies virus (Lyssavirus).

  • Transmission: Bite of infected animals (commonly dogs).

  • Prevention:

    • Immediate wound washing

    • Rabies vaccine

    • Rabies immunoglobulin (when indicated)

  • Clinical features:

    • Hydrophobia

    • Aerophobia

    • Encephalitis

Exam Pearl:
Once clinical rabies develops, mortality is almost 100%; prevention after exposure is the key.

Medicine 09.question: ১২) Which is most common extrapulmonary site of TB?
Medicine 09.exp:
The lymph nodes are the most common site of extrapulmonary tuberculosis (TB). Tuberculous lymphadenitis, also known as scrofula, commonly involves the cervical lymph nodes. Extrapulmonary TB occurs when Mycobacterium tuberculosis spreads from the primary focus through lymphatic or hematogenous routes to other organs. Other extrapulmonary sites include the pleura, meninges, bones, intestine, and genitourinary tract, but lymph nodes are the most frequently affected.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common extrapulmonary TB site: Lymph nodes.

  • Cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis = Scrofula.

  • Other important sites:

    • Pleura

    • CNS (TB meningitis)

    • Bone and joints

    • Genitourinary tract

  • Hematogenous dissemination can cause miliary TB.

Exam Pearl:
Extrapulmonary TB most commonly affects lymph nodes, especially cervical lymph nodes.

Medicine 09.question: ১৩) Which symptom appears at the end of first week of enteric fever?
Medicine 09.exp:
Rose spots are a characteristic clinical feature of enteric (typhoid) fever that typically appear toward the end of the first week of illness. They are small, faint, salmon-colored, blanching macules found mainly on the trunk and abdomen due to bacterial emboli and inflammation of dermal capillaries. Other symptoms such as headache, myalgia, and fever usually occur earlier during the initial phase of infection. Delirium is a feature of more severe or late-stage disease, especially during the third week, due to systemic toxicity.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Rose spots → End of 1st week of typhoid fever.

  • Site: Trunk and abdomen.

  • Causative organism: Salmonella Typhi.

  • Transmission: Fecal-oral route.

  • Complications:

    • Intestinal hemorrhage

    • Ileal perforation

    • Encephalopathy

Exam Pearl:
Typhoid rose spots appear around the end of the first week and are classically seen on the trunk.

Medicine 09.question: ১৪) 8th nerve damage is caused by.......?
Medicine 09.exp:
Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used in tuberculosis treatment and is associated with ototoxicity, causing damage to the 8th cranial nerve (vestibulocochlear nerve). It may produce vestibular toxicity (vertigo, imbalance) and sometimes hearing impairment due to cochlear damage. Isoniazid (INH) commonly causes peripheral neuropathy due to pyridoxine deficiency, ethambutol causes optic neuritis with red-green color blindness, and rifampicin is associated with hepatotoxicity and orange discoloration of body fluids.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Streptomycin → 8th nerve toxicity (ototoxicity).

  • INH → Peripheral neuropathy (prevent with pyridoxine).

  • Ethambutol → Optic neuritis + red-green color blindness.

  • Rifampicin → Hepatotoxicity + orange body fluids.

  • Aminoglycosides commonly cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

Exam Pearl:
TB drug causing 8th nerve damage = Streptomycin.

Medicine 09.question: ১৫) Which disease is transmitted by female anopheles mosquitoes?
Medicine 09.exp:
Malaria is transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito, which acts as the vector for Plasmodium species. During feeding, the mosquito injects sporozoites into the human bloodstream, initiating the liver stage followed by the erythrocytic stage of infection. The major human malaria species include Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. Filaria is mainly transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, dengue by Aedes mosquitoes, and kala-azar by the sandfly (Phlebotomus).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Female Anopheles → Malaria.

  • Causative organism: Plasmodium.

  • Infective form for humans: Sporozoite.

  • Dengue vector: Aedes aegypti.

  • Kala-azar vector: Sandfly (Phlebotomus).

Exam Pearl:
Female Anopheles mosquito is the classic vector of malaria.

Medicine 09.question: ১৬) Saddle break pattern of fever is a clinical feature of which disease?
Medicine 09.exp:
A saddleback (biphasic) fever pattern is a characteristic feature described in dengue fever. The patient initially develops high fever, followed by a brief period of improvement or defervescence, and then experiences a second rise in temperature. This biphasic pattern resembles the shape of a saddle. Dengue is caused by the dengue virus (Flavivirus) and transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. Typhoid usually shows a step-ladder fever pattern, malaria shows intermittent or periodic fever due to parasite cycles, and paratyphoid does not classically show a saddleback pattern.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Dengue → Saddleback (biphasic) fever.

  • Vector: Aedes aegypti mosquito.

  • Dengue features:

    • High fever

    • Severe myalgia ("breakbone fever")

    • Rash

    • Thrombocytopenia

  • Typhoid → Step-ladder fever.

  • Malaria → Intermittent fever pattern.

Exam Pearl:
Saddleback fever pattern is classically associated with dengue fever.

Medicine 09.question: ১৭) What type of malaria is more severe?
Medicine 09.exp:
Plasmodium falciparum malaria is the most severe form of malaria and is responsible for the majority of malaria-related deaths worldwide. It causes severe disease because infected red blood cells develop cytoadherence and sequestration in small blood vessels, leading to tissue ischemia and complications such as cerebral malaria, severe anemia, renal failure, and multi-organ dysfunction. P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae usually cause less severe disease, although they can still produce significant illness. P. vivax and P. ovale can cause relapses due to dormant liver forms (hypnozoites).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • P. falciparum → Most severe malaria.

  • Causes:

    • Cerebral malaria

    • Severe anemia

    • Blackwater fever

    • Organ failure

  • Mechanism of severity: RBC sequestration in microvasculature.

  • P. vivax/P. ovale → Relapse due to hypnozoites.

  • P. malariae → Quartan fever.

Exam Pearl:
Falciparum malaria is the deadliest malaria due to sequestration of infected RBCs and severe complication

Medicine 09.question: ১৮) Which is the best fluid for intravenous replacement in Cholera?
Medicine 09.exp:
Ringer Lactate (RL) is the preferred intravenous fluid for replacement therapy in cholera because it effectively corrects the massive loss of water and electrolytes, especially sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate. Cholera causes profuse watery diarrhea due to cholera toxin–mediated activation of adenylate cyclase, leading to increased chloride secretion and severe dehydration. Ringer Lactate contains lactate, which is metabolized to bicarbonate and helps correct metabolic acidosis associated with dehydration. Normal saline can also be used, especially when RL is unavailable, but RL is considered the best choice.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cholera dehydration → Ringer Lactate is the preferred IV fluid.

  • Cholera toxin → ↑ cAMP → ↑ chloride secretion → watery diarrhea.

  • Severe dehydration requires rapid IV fluid replacement.

  • Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is used for mild to moderate dehydration.

  • RL helps correct associated metabolic acidosis.

Exam Pearl:
Best IV fluid for severe cholera dehydration = Ringer Lactate.

Medicine 09.question: ১৯) What is the duration of continuation phase of category 2 anti-TB treatment?
Medicine 09.exp:
In the classical Category II anti-tuberculosis treatment regimen (for previously treated TB patients such as relapse, treatment after failure, or treatment after default), the regimen consists of an intensive phase of 3 months followed by a continuation phase of 5 months in many older national TB programs. However, in the commonly tested older WHO Category II regimen, the continuation phase is 5 months, making option গ) 5 months the correct answer. The continuation phase generally includes rifampicin, isoniazid, and ethambutol. The category system has been updated in many guidelines, but exam questions often refer to the traditional regimen.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Traditional Category II regimen:

    • Intensive phase: 3 months

    • Continuation phase: 5 months

  • Total duration: 8 months.

  • Drugs commonly used: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol + Streptomycin initially.

  • Current TB programs increasingly use individualized or shorter WHO-recommended regimens.

Exam Pearl:
Category II TB treatment continuation pha

Medicine 09.question: ২০) Giemsa stained thick and thin blood film are prepared for diagnosis of which disease?
Medicine 09.exp:
Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films are the standard microscopic methods for diagnosis of malaria. The thick film is more sensitive for detecting parasites because it concentrates blood and allows examination of a larger volume, while the thin film helps identify the Plasmodium species and assess parasitemia. The parasite is seen inside red blood cells, with characteristic forms such as trophozoites, schizonts, and gametocytes. Filaria is diagnosed by detecting microfilariae in blood films (often timed with periodicity), dengue by antigen/serology tests, and kala-azar by detection of Leishmania amastigotes in tissue aspirates.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Malaria diagnosis → Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood smear.

  • Thick film → Detection of parasite.

  • Thin film → Species identification.

  • Malaria parasite: Plasmodium species.

  • Falciparum → crescent-shaped gametocytes.

Exam Pearl:
Thick and thin Giemsa blood films are classic diagnostic tests for malaria.

Medicine 09.question: ২১) Persistent chronic carriage state of enteric fever occurs in which organ?
Medicine 09.exp:
The gallbladder is the main site responsible for the persistent chronic carrier state of enteric (typhoid) fever. After infection with Salmonella Typhi, some individuals continue to shed bacteria in stool for prolonged periods due to colonization of the gallbladder, especially when gallstones are present. These chronic carriers act as important sources of transmission. The organism may persist in the biliary tract due to biofilm formation on gallstones. The intestine, liver, and kidney are not the classical sites of chronic carriage.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Chronic typhoid carrier state → Gallbladder.

  • Organism: Salmonella Typhi.

  • Risk factor: Gallstones.

  • Chronic carriers shed bacteria in feces.

  • Classic example: “Typhoid Mary” (chronic carrier).

Exam Pearl:
Salmonella Typhi hides in the gallbladder and causes chronic carriage.

Medicine 09.question: ২২) What is the usual duration of chemoprophylaxis of malaria with chloroquine?
Medicine 09.exp:
The usual duration of chloroquine chemoprophylaxis for malaria is 4 weeks after leaving the endemic area because chloroquine has activity mainly against the blood stages of Plasmodium and does not completely eliminate dormant liver stages (hypnozoites). Chloroquine is traditionally taken weekly, starting before travel and continued for 4 weeks after return from a malaria-endemic region. It is mainly effective against chloroquine-sensitive malaria, especially Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale (blood stages), but resistance limits its use in many regions.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Chloroquine prophylaxis → Continue for 4 weeks after exposure.

  • Chloroquine dosing is typically weekly.

  • Does not eradicate hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale.

  • Drug resistance is common in P. falciparum.

  • Alternative prophylactic drugs include doxycycline, mefloquine, and atovaquone-proguanil.

Exam Pearl:
Malaria chemoprophylaxis with chloroquine is continued for 4 weeks after leaving the endemic area.

Medicine 09.question: ২৩) Which is the most important diagnostic method for enteric fever?
Medicine 09.exp:
Blood culture is the most important and preferred diagnostic method for enteric (typhoid) fever, especially during the first week of illness, because Salmonella Typhi is present in the bloodstream during this phase. Isolation of the organism from blood provides definitive diagnosis. Stool culture may become positive later in the disease but is less sensitive in the early phase. CBC may show nonspecific findings such as leukopenia, and imaging has no primary role in diagnosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Best diagnostic test for early typhoid fever: Blood culture.

  • Organism: Salmonella Typhi.

  • Stool culture becomes more useful in later stages.

  • Chronic carrier state → organism persists in gallbladder.

  • Widal test indicates antibodies but has limited diagnostic accuracy.

Exam Pearl:
First week of enteric fever = Blood culture is the diagnostic test of choice.

Medicine 09.question: ২৪) Which is the 1st sign of kala azar?
Medicine 09.exp:
The first and most characteristic sign of kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is usually splenomegaly. The disease is caused by Leishmania donovani, which infects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to marked enlargement of the spleen, liver, and lymph nodes. Fever is a common symptom, but splenic enlargement is the earliest and most prominent physical finding. Blackening of skin (classically described as “kala-azar,” meaning black fever) is a late feature due to hyperpigmentation and is not the first sign.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kala-azar = Visceral leishmaniasis.

  • Causative organism: Leishmania donovani.

  • Vector: Sandfly (Phlebotomus).

  • Earliest prominent sign: Splenomegaly.

  • Features:

    • Prolonged fever

    • Hepatosplenomegaly

    • Pancytopenia

    • Hyperpigmentation

Exam Pearl:
In kala-azar, early marked splenomegaly is the classic first physical sign.

Medicine 09.question: ২৫) Treatment of enteric fever should be continued for how many days?
Medicine 09.exp:
The usual duration of treatment for enteric (typhoid) fever is 14 days, depending on the antibiotic used, severity of illness, and local resistance patterns. Adequate duration is important to achieve eradication of Salmonella Typhi and reduce relapse and carrier states. Commonly used antibiotics include ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and fluoroquinolones (where sensitive). Shorter courses may be effective with some newer regimens, but the classic exam answer for uncomplicated enteric fever treatment duration is 14 days.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Enteric fever organism: Salmonella Typhi.

  • Classic treatment duration: 14 days.

  • Chronic carrier state → Gallbladder.

  • Diagnosis:

    • Early illness → Blood culture

    • Later illness → Stool culture may become positive.

  • Transmission: Fecal-oral route.

Exam Pearl:
Traditional exam answer: Typhoid treatment is continued for 14 days.

Medicine 09.question: ২৬) What is the most dominant feature of kala azar?
Medicine 09.exp:
The most dominant hematological feature of kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is pancytopenia, which occurs due to involvement of the reticuloendothelial system and bone marrow suppression/hypersplenism. The infection caused by Leishmania donovani leads to enlargement of the spleen and increased destruction/sequestration of blood cells, resulting in decreased red cells, white cells, and platelets. Other findings may include prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, hypergammaglobulinemia, and hypoalbuminemia. Isolated granulocytopenia or monocytosis is not the typical dominant finding.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kala-azar → Pancytopenia.

  • Cause: Splenic sequestration + bone marrow involvement.

  • Classic features:

    • Prolonged fever

    • Massive splenomegaly

    • Weight loss

    • Hyperpigmentation

    • Pancytopenia

  • Organism: Leishmania donovani.

Exam Pearl:
Visceral leishmaniasis classically presents with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia.

Medicine 09.question: ২৭) Which should be avoided in dengue?
Medicine 09.exp:
Aspirin should be avoided in dengue because it inhibits platelet function and can increase the risk of bleeding complications in a disease already associated with thrombocytopenia and increased vascular fragility. Dengue fever is managed mainly with supportive treatment, including careful fluid management and antipyretics such as paracetamol for fever control. Corticosteroids and antivirals are not routinely recommended in dengue. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including aspirin, should be avoided due to bleeding risk.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Dengue → Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs.

  • Preferred antipyretic: Paracetamol.

  • Dengue features:

    • Fever

    • Myalgia

    • Thrombocytopenia

    • Plasma leakage in severe disease

  • Vector: Aedes aegypti.

  • Treatment: Mainly supportive care.

Exam Pearl:
Dengue + aspirin = increased bleeding risk; use paracetamol instead.

Medicine 09.question: ২৮) rk39 strip test is done in....?
Medicine 09.exp:
The rK39 strip test is a rapid diagnostic test used for visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar). It detects antibodies against the rK39 antigen, which is derived from a kinesin-related protein of Leishmania donovani. It is a simple, rapid, and widely used test for diagnosis, especially in endemic areas. The test detects the host immune response rather than directly identifying the parasite. Malaria, dengue, and filariasis require different diagnostic methods.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • rK39 strip test → Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis).

  • Causative organism: Leishmania donovani.

  • Vector: Sandfly (Phlebotomus).

  • Common features:

    • Massive splenomegaly

    • Prolonged fever

    • Pancytopenia

    • Hyperpigmentation

  • Diagnostic methods:

    • rK39 antibody test

    • Demonstration of amastigotes in tissue aspirate

Exam Pearl:
rK39 rapid test is a classic diagnostic test for kala-azar.

Medicine 09.question: ২৯) Diarrhoea longer than 5 days is suggestive of....... in origin?
Medicine 09.exp:
Diarrhea lasting more than 5 days is suggestive of a protozoal cause, especially in the context of persistent diarrhea. Protozoal infections such as Giardiasis and Amoebiasis commonly produce prolonged or persistent diarrhea due to intestinal mucosal involvement. Viral diarrhea is usually acute and self-limiting, often resolving within a few days. Bacterial diarrhea is commonly acute but may persist depending on the organism and host factors. Fungal diarrhea is uncommon and usually occurs in immunocompromised patients.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Persistent diarrhea (>5 days) → Think protozoal infection.

  • Common protozoal causes:

    • Giardia lamblia → Greasy, foul-smelling diarrhea, malabsorption

    • Entamoeba histolytica → Bloody diarrhea/dysentery

  • Viral diarrhea → Usually acute and self-limited.

  • Bacterial diarrhea → Often associated with fever, blood, or inflammatory features.

Exam Pearl:
Diarrhea lasting beyond several days classically suggests a protozoal etiology, especially Giardia or Entamoeba.

Medicine 09.question: ৩০) The average adult's diarrhoeal stool accounts for loss of 200 ml of......... fluid?
Medicine 09.exp:
The average adult diarrhoeal stool is considered to cause loss of approximately 200 mL of isotonic fluid. In most diarrheal illnesses, the intestinal fluid loss contains water and electrolytes in proportions that are relatively similar to plasma, leading to isotonic dehydration. This results in loss of both extracellular fluid volume and electrolytes, especially sodium and chloride. Severe diarrheal diseases such as cholera can cause massive isotonic fluid loss, leading to hypovolemia and shock if not corrected. Hypotonic and hypertonic fluid losses occur in specific conditions but are not the typical pattern in acute diarrhea.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Diarrheal fluid loss is usually isotonic.

  • Major electrolyte loss:

    • Sodium

    • Chloride

    • Bicarbonate

    • Potassium

  • Severe diarrhea → dehydration → hypovolemic shock.

  • ORS works by sodium-glucose cotransport in the intestine.

Exam Pearl:
Diarrhea causes mainly isotonic fluid loss with extracellula

Medicine 09.question: ৩১) Which is the most common cause of antimicrobial associated diarrhoea?
Medicine 09.exp:
The most common cause of antimicrobial-associated diarrhea (AAD) is Clostridioides difficile (formerly Clostridium difficile). Antibiotic use disrupts the normal intestinal flora, allowing overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B. These toxins cause mucosal injury, inflammation, and diarrhea that may range from mild diarrhea to severe pseudomembranous colitis. Common antibiotics associated with C. difficile infection include clindamycin, broad-spectrum penicillins, cephalosporins, and fluoroquinolones. E. coli, B. cereus, and rotavirus are not the classic causes of antibiotic-associated diarrhea.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Antibiotic-associated diarrhea → C. difficile.

  • Toxins:

    • Toxin A → Enterotoxin

    • Toxin B → Cytotoxin

  • Causes pseudomembranous colitis.

  • Risk factors:

    • Recent antibiotic use

    • Hospitalization

    • Elderly/immunocompromised patients

  • Diagnosis: Detection of C. difficile toxins or toxin genes.

Exam Pearl:
Recent antibiotic use + diarrhea = think Clostridioides difficile.

Medicine 09.question: ৩২) Which anti-TB drug acts on DNA transcription?
Medicine 09.exp:
Rifampicin acts on DNA transcription by inhibiting the DNA-dependent RNA polymerase of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This blocks the synthesis of bacterial RNA and leads to inhibition of protein production, making it a powerful bactericidal anti-TB drug. Isoniazid (INH) inhibits mycolic acid synthesis in the bacterial cell wall, ethambutol inhibits arabinosyl transferase affecting cell wall formation, and streptomycin inhibits protein synthesis by acting on the 30S ribosomal subunit.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Rifampicin → Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase → blocks transcription.

  • INH → Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis.

  • Ethambutol → Inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis.

  • Streptomycin → 30S ribosomal inhibition → protein synthesis inhibition.

  • Rifampicin causes orange-red discoloration of body fluids.

Exam Pearl:
Anti-TB drug acting on transcription = Rifampicin (RNA polymerase inhibitor).

Medicine 09.question: ৩৩) LD body is diagnostic for......?
Medicine 09.exp:
LD bodies (Leishman-Donovan bodies) are the intracellular forms of Leishmania donovani found inside macrophages and are diagnostic of kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis). They represent amastigote forms of the parasite and can be demonstrated in tissue aspirates, especially splenic, bone marrow, or lymph node aspirates. The organisms appear as small round bodies with a nucleus and kinetoplast. Malaria is diagnosed by blood smear showing Plasmodium species, dengue by antigen/serology tests, and filaria by detection of microfilariae.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • LD bodies → Kala-azar.

  • LD body = Leishmania donovani amastigote.

  • Found inside macrophages.

  • Diagnostic samples:

    • Splenic aspirate

    • Bone marrow aspirate

    • Lymph node aspirate

  • Vector: Sandfly (Phlebotomus).

Exam Pearl:
Leishman-Donovan bodies inside macrophages = Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).

Medicine 09.question: ৩৪) Which is not a 1st line drug for kala azar treatment?
Medicine 09.exp:
Sodium stibogluconate is an antimonial drug that was historically used for kala-azar treatment but is no longer considered a preferred first-line drug in many regions due to high resistance and toxicity. Current first-line treatments for visceral leishmaniasis include:

  • Liposomal amphotericin B → preferred in many guidelines

  • Miltefosine → oral antileishmanial drug

  • Paromomycin → aminoglycoside used in some endemic areas

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) → Leishmania donovani

  • First-line drugs:

    • Liposomal amphotericin B

    • Miltefosine

    • Paromomycin

  • Sodium stibogluconate → old drug, resistance/toxicity problem

Exam Pearl:

Medicine 09.question: ৩৫) Retrobulbar neuritis is an adverse reaction of.....?
Medicine 09.exp:
Ethambutol causes retrobulbar neuritis (optic neuritis) as a major adverse effect. It affects the optic nerve, leading to decreased visual acuity and red-green color blindness due to impaired optic nerve function. The toxicity is dose- and duration-dependent and is usually reversible if detected early and the drug is stopped.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ethambutol → Optic neuritis + red-green color blindness

  • INH → Peripheral neuropathy (prevent with pyridoxine)

  • Rifampicin → Hepatotoxicity + orange discoloration of body fluids

  • Streptomycin → 8th cranial nerve toxicity (ototoxicity)

Exam Pearl:
Retrobulbar neuritis in anti-TB therapy = Ethambutol.

Medicine 09.question: ৩৬) A 30 years old female from the northern zone with unilateral leg swelling which is non pitting. what may be possible diagnosis?
Medicine 09.exp:
A 30-year-old female with unilateral, non-pitting leg swelling from a tropical endemic area is suggestive of lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis). The swelling occurs due to obstruction of lymphatic vessels by adult filarial worms, leading to chronic lymphedema. It is commonly caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and transmitted by mosquitoes (mainly Culex).

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Filaria → Non-pitting lymphedema (elephantiasis).

  • Common organism: Wuchereria bancrofti.

  • Vector: Mosquito (commonly Culex).

  • Features:

    • Unilateral limb swelling

    • Thickened skin

    • Lymphatic obstruction

  • Malaria → intermittent fever, not chronic limb swelling.

  • Dengue → fever, thrombocytopenia, rash.

  • Rabies → encephalitis after animal bite.

Exam Pearl:
Chronic unilateral non-pitting leg swelling in an endemic area = Lymphatic filariasis.

Medicine 09.question: ৩৭) Stages of PKDL excludes.......?
Medicine 09.exp:
Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a complication that occurs after treatment of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar). It typically progresses through three skin lesion stages:

  1. Macular stage → flat, hypopigmented patches

  2. Papular stage → raised papules

  3. Nodular stage → nodules

Pustular (pastular) stage is not a recognized stage of PKDL.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • PKDL stages: Macular → Papular → Nodular

  • Occurs after kala-azar treatment

  • Caused by persistence of Leishmania donovani in the skin

  • Important because patients can act as a reservoir of infection

Exam Pearl:
PKDL does not have a pustular stage.

Medicine 09.question: ৩৮) Anti tubercular drugs excludes......?
Medicine 09.exp:
Dapsone is not an anti-tubercular drug. It is mainly used in the treatment of leprosy (Hansen’s disease), especially as part of multidrug therapy for Mycobacterium leprae.

The major first-line anti-TB drugs include:

  • INH (Isoniazid) → inhibits mycolic acid synthesis

  • Rifampicin → inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase

  • Streptomycin → inhibits protein synthesis (30S ribosome)

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • TB drugs: INH, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol, Streptomycin

  • Dapsone → Leprosy drug (anti-mycobacterial for M. leprae)

Exam Pearl:
Dapsone is not an anti-TB drug; it is used for leprosy.

Medicine 09.question: ৩৯) Which disease is related to sandfly?
Medicine 09.exp:
The sandfly (Phlebotomus) is the vector responsible for transmission of kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis). The causative organism is Leishmania donovani, which is transmitted when an infected female sandfly bites humans.

Other vector associations:

  • Malaria → Female Anopheles mosquito

  • Dengue → Aedes mosquito

  • Filaria → Mosquito (commonly Culex)

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Sandfly → Kala-azar

  • Organism: Leishmania donovani

  • Diagnostic findings:

    • LD bodies in macrophages

    • rK39 test positive

  • Features:

    • Massive splenomegaly

    • Fever

    • Pancytopenia

Exam Pearl:
Sandfly bite causing visceral leishmaniasis = Kala-azar.

Medicine 09.question: ৪০) What is the loading dose of artesunate in malaria?
Medicine 09.exp:
The loading dose of artesunate for severe malaria in adults is 2.4 mg/kg intravenously (IV) given initially, followed by further doses at scheduled intervals. Artesunate is a rapidly acting artemisinin derivative that reduces parasite biomass quickly and is the preferred treatment for severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Severe malaria → IV artesunate

  • Loading dose: 2.4 mg/kg IV

  • Mechanism: Generates free radicals that damage parasite proteins and membranes.

  • Most severe malaria species: Plasmodium falciparum

  • Alternative (where IV access unavailable): IM artesunate.

Exam Pearl:
Artesunate loading dose in severe malaria = 2.4 mg/kg IV.

Medicine 09.question: ৪১) Which is most common rabid animal?
Medicine 09.exp:
The dog is the most common rabid animal responsible for human rabies transmission worldwide. Rabies is caused by the rabies virus (a Lyssavirus) and is usually transmitted through the bite or saliva of an infected animal. In many countries, domestic dogs remain the major reservoir and source of human infection.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common source of human rabies → Rabid dog

  • Virus: Rabies virus (Lyssavirus)

  • Transmission: Animal bite/saliva contamination

  • Rabies → almost 100% fatal once symptoms appear

  • Prevention: Post-exposure prophylaxis (vaccine ± rabies immunoglobulin)

Exam Pearl:
Dog is the most common rabid animal causing human rabies.

Medicine 09.question: ৪২) For radical cure of malaria which drug is mainly used in combination with chloroquine?
Medicine 09.exp:
Primaquine is used with chloroquine for the radical cure of malaria, especially in Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale infections. Chloroquine clears the blood-stage parasites, while primaquine eliminates the dormant liver hypnozoites, preventing relapse. Before giving primaquine, G6PD deficiency should be excluded because it can cause hemolytic anemia in affected individuals.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Radical cure of malaria → Primaquine

  • Chloroquine → kills erythrocytic (blood) stages

  • Primaquine → kills hepatic hypnozoites

  • Hypnozoites present in:

    • P. vivax

    • P. ovale

  • Check G6PD level before primaquine therapy.

Exam Pearl:
Chloroquine + Primaquine = radical cure of vivax malaria.

Medicine 09.question: ৪৩) Elephantiasis is a feature of which disease?
Medicine 09.exp:
Elephantiasis is a classic feature of lymphatic filariasis, caused mainly by Wuchereria bancrofti. The adult worms block lymphatic vessels, causing chronic lymphedema, which leads to massive enlargement and thickening of limbs or genitalia.

Other options:

  • Malaria → fever with chills and anemia

  • Rabies → encephalitis with neurological symptoms

  • Dengue → fever, rash, thrombocytopenia

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Elephantiasis → Lymphatic filariasis

  • Organism: Wuchereria bancrofti

  • Vector: Mosquito (commonly Culex)

  • Pathology: Lymphatic obstruction → non-pitting edema

Exam Pearl:
Elephantiasis is a hallmark of filarial infection.

Medicine 09.question: ৪৪) Which marker is significant for diagnosis of TB in pleural fluid?
Medicine 09.exp:
Adenosine deaminase (ADA) level in pleural fluid is an important diagnostic marker for tuberculous pleural effusion. Increased ADA activity reflects activation of T-lymphocytes in response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A high pleural fluid ADA level strongly supports the diagnosis of pleural TB, especially in endemic areas.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pleural fluid TB marker → ADA

  • ADA is produced mainly by activated T lymphocytes and macrophages.

  • Pleural TB fluid is usually:

    • Exudative

    • Lymphocyte predominant

    • Increased ADA

  • Confirmatory test: Demonstration of M. tuberculosis (culture/GeneXpert where available).

Exam Pearl:
Raised pleural fluid ADA = suggestive of tuberculous pleural effusion.

Medicine 09.question: ৪৫) How many doses of human diploid cell vaccine is given for rabies?
Medicine 09.exp:
Human diploid cell vaccine (HDCV) for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis is commonly given as 4 doses in the Essen regimen:

  • Day 0 (first dose)

  • Day 3

  • Day 7

  • Day 14

(An additional dose on Day 28 may be given in some immunocompromised patients.)

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Rabies vaccine (HDCV) → 4 doses (0, 3, 7, 14 days)

  • Severe exposure (Category III) → Vaccine + Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG)

  • Once clinical rabies symptoms appear → almost 100% fatal

Exam Pearl:
Human diploid cell vaccine schedule = 4 doses.

Medicine 09.question: ৪৬) Which is not a macroscopic finding of bacillary dysentery?
Medicine 09.exp:
Bacillary dysentery (shigellosis) typically produces small-volume, frequent stools containing blood and mucus with little or no fecal matter. The stool is often offensive/foul smelling, not odourless.

Macroscopic features of bacillary dysentery:

  • Blood and mucus present

  • Small quantity of stool

  • Bright red blood may be seen

  • Little or no fecal matter

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Bacillary dysentery → Shigella

  • Stool: blood + mucus + pus cells

  • Usually small volume, unlike cholera (large-volume watery stool)

  • Causes:

    • Fever

    • Abdominal cramps

    • Tenesmus

Exam Pearl:
Odourless stool is NOT a feature of bacillary dysentery.

Medicine 09.question: ৪৭) Coated tongue with relative bradycardia signifies......?
Medicine 09.exp:
A coated tongue with relative bradycardia (Faget sign) is a classic feature of enteric (typhoid) fever caused by Salmonella Typhi. Relative bradycardia means the pulse rate is lower than expected for the degree of fever.

Other features of enteric fever:

  • Sustained fever

  • Toxic look

  • Coated tongue

  • Abdominal discomfort

  • Rose spots on trunk (usually in the second week)

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Relative bradycardia → Enteric fever

  • Organism: Salmonella Typhi

  • Transmission: Fecal–oral route

  • Chronic carrier site: Gallbladder

  • Diagnostic test: Blood culture (early stage)

Exam Pearl:
Coated tongue + relative bradycardia = Typhoid (enteric fever).

Medicine 09.question: ৪৮) Which is treatment of choice in lymphatic filariasis?
Medicine 09.exp:
Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the treatment of choice for lymphatic filariasis. It is effective against microfilariae and some adult worms of filarial parasites, especially Wuchereria bancrofti.

Other drugs:

  • Ivermectin → commonly used in mass drug administration programs and has strong microfilaricidal activity.

  • Albendazole → often combined with DEC or ivermectin in control programs.

  • Corticosteroids → used only for inflammatory/allergic complications, not as primary treatment.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Lymphatic filariasis → DEC (drug of choice)

  • Organism: Wuchereria bancrofti

  • Feature: Elephantiasis (chronic lymphedema)

  • Vector: Mosquito

Exam Pearl:
Drug of choice for filariasis = Diethylcarbamazine (DEC).

Medicine 09.question: ৪৯) Hypopigmented patch with ulner nerve thickening indicates........?
Medicine 09.exp:
A hypopigmented skin patch with thickening of the ulnar nerve is a classic feature of leprosy (Hansen’s disease) caused by Mycobacterium leprae. The organism affects peripheral nerves, causing sensory loss and nerve enlargement, especially the ulnar nerve.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Leprosy triad:

    1. Hypopigmented/anaesthetic skin lesion

    2. Thickened peripheral nerve

    3. Acid-fast bacilli in skin smear (in multibacillary cases)

  • Commonly affected nerves:

    • Ulnar nerve

    • Common peroneal nerve

    • Greater auricular nerve

Exam Pearl:
Hypopigmented patch + thickened ulnar nerve = Leprosy.

Medicine 09.question: ৫০) What is the finding of CXR of PTB patient?
Medicine 09.exp:
In pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB), chest X-ray commonly shows patchy opacities/infiltrates, especially in the upper lobes in post-primary (secondary) TB. Other findings may include cavitation, fibrosis, volume loss, and nodules.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • PTB CXR → Patchy opacity (common finding)

  • Post-primary TB:

    • Upper lobe involvement

    • Cavitation

    • Fibrosis

  • Miliary TB:

    • Multiple tiny “millet seed” nodules

Exam Pearl:
Pulmonary TB classically produces patchy opacities on CXR.
